title: Immigration Compliance Becomes the New Dealbreaker in Corporate M&A
excerpt: As federal enforcement intensifies, acquirers are discovering that inherited workforce irregularities can tank transactions — pushing immigration due diligence from checklist item to deal-critical priority.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Immigration compliance is now a critical risk factor in M&A transactions due to heightened enforcement.
  • The U.S. lost 750,000 foreign-born workers in early 2026, increasing acquisition risks.
  • Stricter visa enforcement is driving companies to acquire smaller firms for talent access.
  • Buyers face fines of $288 to $2,861 per I-9 violation, impacting deal structures.
  • The FY 2027 H-1B cap closed, complicating talent acquisition for companies.

A Fortune 100 company earlier this year bought a small construction operation in Utah, then asked immigration counsel to review the workforce documentation. The result: 98% of the acquired company's workers were undocumented. "You're telling us that this acquisition was entirely worthless?" the buyer asked, according to Chris Thomas, partner at Holland & Hart LLP. His answer was yes.

The case, reported by Bloomberg Law, is an extreme example of a pattern that immigration attorneys say has become routine in 2026. Under heightened federal enforcement — expanded I-9 audits, increased site visits by USCIS and ICE, and new Department of Labor investigations into H-1B practices — immigration compliance has moved from a due diligence afterthought to a factor that can delay, diminish, or outright kill a transaction.

The Enforcement Shift

The scale of change is measurable. The U.S. labor force lost 750,000 foreign-born workers in the first half of 2026 alone, according to Pew Research, as the Trump administration made curbing immigration a centerpiece of its domestic agenda. Raids on companies suspected of employing undocumented workers have increased, and the Department of Labor has unveiled plans to investigate corporate H-1B visa practices.

"I don't think we've seen immigration enforcement in the last 60 years look like it does now."

— Mark Pendleton, Partner, Bradley Arant Boult Cummings LLP

The information technology and financial sectors — two of the largest sponsors of H-1B visas — were also the top dealmaking industries globally last quarter, according to S&P Global, placing immigration compliance directly at the intersection of the two biggest trends shaping corporate America.

Deal Structure Determines Exposure

As Reuters detailed in a recent analysis, the legal architecture of a transaction dictates how immigration risk flows to the buyer. In a stock purchase, the target company continues as the same legal entity, so existing visa petitions, Labor Condition Applications, and I-9 records remain intact. In a statutory merger, the surviving entity can claim successor-in-interest status and inherit immigration filings.

But asset purchases — often preferred for tax and liability reasons — are the most treacherous. Immigration obligations do not transfer by default. Each affected employee's H-1B petition, labor certification, or pending green card case may need to be refiled from scratch, subject to USCIS processing times that can leave critical workers unable to start on day one.

The risks extend across every major visa category. L-1 intracompany transferee eligibility can be destroyed if an acquisition severs the qualifying corporate relationship between U.S. and foreign entities. E-1 and E-2 treaty visas — which require the enterprise to be at least 50% owned by nationals of a treaty country — can vanish overnight if a company of a different nationality acquires the business. Even F-1 students on STEM OPT can lose authorization if a gap appears in E-Verify participation during a corporate transition.

The Acqui-Hire Response

The enforcement crackdown is producing a paradoxical side effect. Research by Wharton professor Exequiel Hernandez and colleagues, analyzing data from nearly 3,900 U.S. firms that used H-1B visas between 2001 and 2020, found that when visa caps shrink or enforcement tightens, affected companies are significantly more likely to acquire other firms — often smaller ones — to secure talent they can no longer hire directly.

These "acqui-hires" have become a workaround for companies dependent on foreign engineers, scientists, and software developers. U.S. technology firms completed 3,113 mergers and acquisitions in the first half of 2025, a 36% increase from the same period in 2024, according to Corum Group — a trend that has continued into 2026.

"It definitely has the potential to kill a deal. Some buyers are aggressive and buying up companies without being acquainted with workforce realities."

— Mary Kate Fernandez, Business Immigration Attorney, Adams & Reese

The H-1B Factor

Compounding the challenge, the FY 2027 H-1B cap has officially closed after USCIS received enough petitions to fill all 85,000 available slots, including the 20,000 U.S. advanced-degree exemption. This year marked the first under a new wage-weighted lottery system, which significantly favored higher-paid positions: 71.5% of selected beneficiaries held U.S. advanced degrees, up from 57% the previous year, while only 17.7% of selections went to the lowest prevailing wage category.

With no second lottery planned, employers that missed the cap must wait until the FY 2028 registration period in spring 2027 — or pursue alternative strategies including O-1 extraordinary ability visas, L-1 intracompany transfers, and direct green card sponsorship.

Impact on Indian Professionals

For Indian nationals — who constitute the largest share of H-1B recipients and face the longest green card backlogs — the consequences ripple through every corporate transaction. An acquisition that disrupts a pending EB-2 or EB-3 green card application can reset years, sometimes more than a decade, of waiting in the employment-based backlog. Post-transaction layoffs can trigger additional complications, as employers must withdraw LCAs and petitions for terminated workers, and laid-off H-1B holders receive only a 60-day grace period to find new sponsorship.

Immigration attorneys report that companies are now engaging counsel far earlier in the deal process. As Adams & Reese's Fernandez noted, one buyer this summer forced the seller to rehire employees before the deal closed to ensure compliance — extending the timeline by months.

What Comes Next

With Deloitte projecting both the value and number of M&A deals to increase over the next year, the immigration compliance burden will only grow. Leading employers are diversifying their strategies — combining H-1B planning with alternative visa categories, remote work arrangements, international assignments, and permanent residence sponsorship.

But the fundamental tension remains: in a market where talent acquisition increasingly drives dealmaking, the regulatory apparatus governing that talent has never been more aggressive. Companies that treat immigration compliance as an afterthought risk not only fines — which can reach $95 million for systematic I-9 violations — but the discovery that the workforce they just acquired cannot legally work for them.
